title: OpenAI models move into chip design: Jalapeño area drops 13%, AMD flagship GPU gains up to 14%
summary: If you thought AI only wrote code and prose, OpenAI just showed another path: models directly editing chip circuits. Its in-house inference chip Jalapeño saved 13% area in key blocks, and work with AMD delivered up to 14% gains on a flagship GPU.
ai_summary: On November 18, 2026, OpenAI published research showing its models directly edit chip circuits—saving area on its first in-house inference chip, Jalapeño, and working with AMD to optimize its next-generation flagship GPU and CPU. Key numbers: Jalapeño's vector unit area fell about 13% and its matrix unit about 10%; AMD's flagship GPU IP improved by up to 14% over heavily optimized baselines; and the models compressed roughly a year of progress into under five months. The evaluation used two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores, with GPT-6.2 Astra posting the highest average score at a budget of about 112,000 tokens. It's aimed at chip design teams and anyone tracking AI capabilities. The biggest caveat: these are OpenAI's self-reported results and haven't been independently reproduced.
brief: On Jalapeño, model-driven changes cut standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and about 10% in the matrix unit, and were confirmed during silicon bring-up.

With AMD: flagship GPU IP improved by up to 14% relative to heavily optimized baselines; roughly a year of progress was completed in under five months, and some changes have already been sent for manufacturing.

At a budget of about 112,000 tokens, GPT-6.2 Astra had the highest average score across the two open-source RISC-V core evaluations; when designing a core from a spec, it scored about 0.7 on PicoRV32 and about 0.75 on Ibex.
Next up: training GPT-Synopsys with Synopsys so the model can use EDA tools the way expert chip designers do.

sections.h: What this is: OpenAI models directly edit chip circuits

blocks.p: On November 18, 2026, OpenAI published research titled "Advancing chip design with OpenAI models." The models here are its GPT-series large models, and what they do is revise a chip's circuit design for engineers rather than design the chip itself.

For context: in August, OpenAI said engineers had used frontier models to speed up development of its first in-house inference chip, Jalapeño. This post fills in the details: what the models changed, the results from working with AMD, and how two open-source RISC-V cores serve as a test for how much each model generation improves.

First, a common chip industry term: PPA stands for power, performance, and area. The core of chip design optimization is making a chip faster, more efficient, and smaller. Every "gain" or "reduction" below refers to those three.
OpenAI began using GPT-o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. The model wasn't new, but it already found some nontrivial PPA improvements.

The improvements are concentrated in two compute blocks. The vector unit manages and executes parallel computing tasks; its area savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored alternative logic implementations and ways to reassign computations across pipeline stages, allowing them to share hardware and cut intermediate storage.

The matrix unit is an arithmetic component, and its improvements came from floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. Two individual redesigns stand out. One multiplier redesign reduced cell area used in synthesis by about 15% while cutting latency from two clock cycles to one. Another adder redesign also reduced cell area by about 15%, while keeping its two-cycle latency unchanged.
Added together, OpenAI estimates the standard-cell area fell about 13% in the vector unit and about 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were confirmed during Jalapeño's silicon bring-up.

blocks.p: The AMD work is more telling because it applies the models to a third-party vendor's flagship product that is already highly optimized. OpenAI says that, relative to "heavily optimized baselines," the models delivered up to 14% PPA improvement on AMD's flagship GPU IP. Note that 14% is the ceiling, and the comparison is not against a rough first version but against a baseline that was already tuned hard.

The method is to rewrite the code that describes chip circuits—SystemVerilog RTL, a hardware description language engineers use to specify how each block behaves. OpenAI says the model reasons about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect, able to rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data.

On speed, OpenAI says this amounts to roughly a year of progress completed in under five months, which it calls unprecedented at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for future versions.

Beyond the GPU, AMD verified single-digit percentage PPA gains across key blocks of its next-generation flagship CPU, using designs written by OpenAI models. After each rewrite, the model used Synopsys tools to verify that behavior was unchanged and to evaluate power, performance, and area trade-offs.

sections.h: How much have the models improved? Two open-source RISC-V cores as the test

blocks.p: Jalapeño and the AMD chips are production designs, so it is hard to fairly quantify how much better each model generation gets. OpenAI therefore set up two open-source cores as a standard test: PicoRV32 and Ibex. Both are 32-bit RISC-V processor cores for embedded, microcontroller-class workloads. PicoRV32 is compact and aimed at FPGAs, while Ibex is used in the OpenTitan security chip.

The task is simple: improve throughput—the number of instructions the core can execute per second. The scoring method matters, because it determines how to read the results. After a model revises a design, the output is checked in simulation. If it fails a check, or uses more than 16 times the original core's area, the run scores zero. Passing designs are measured on workloads the models have never seen, using instructions per clock cycle (IPC). The geometric mean across those workloads is multiplied by the maximum clock frequency estimated with the open-source Yosys tool to estimate instructions per second. For each core, the best throughput observed under the same constraints is scored 1.0; the charts show average scores across runs, including the zeroes.

The result: at a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens, GPT-6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores; GPT-6.1 Sol also outscored GPT-5.6 Sol. On the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT-6.2 Astra's score at about 112,000 tokens is roughly twice GPT-6 Astra's. On Ibex, GPT-6.2 Astra's mean score keeps climbing as the budget grows.

sections.h: Designing a core from a spec: scores actually get higher

blocks.p: The second task is closer to designing from scratch: the model gets only written requirements and templates, then decides how data flows through the core and how to divide the work into stages. The correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput targets are the same as in the previous task.

The result is striking: at about 112,000 tokens, all five models scored higher when designing a core from written requirements than when improving an existing design—on both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT-6.2 Astra improved more on Ibex than on PicoRV32.

Specific scores: starting from the PicoRV32 spec, GPT-6.2 Astra averages 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two budget levels. Starting from the Ibex spec, it averages about 0.75 near the same budget, and its curve stays above the other models. The full evaluation includes 9,881 scored runs.

OpenAI also flags a limitation: when starting from written requirements, models can omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features do little for throughput on the test workloads, which may explain part of the score advantage. Requiring them, tightening the area limit, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test closer to real production design.

list: Cost: the announcement doesn't say how much it cost to modify AMD designs or license Synopsys EDA tools.
Jalapeño's absolute specs: only area reduction percentages are given, not absolute area, frequency, power, or other raw numbers.
Only four of the five evaluated models are named: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6.2 Astra. The fifth model's name isn't disclosed.
The announcement describes the score curves textually but doesn't publish per-model numbers at each token budget.
No direct comparison with human expert designs is provided.
The announcement says only "some" AMD changes were sent for manufacturing, without specifying which ones or which product version will use them.

blocks.p: The value: for chip design teams, the most direct takeaway is a repeatable path—have the model rewrite RTL, verify with EDA tools that behavior is unchanged, and still find PPA gains of anywhere from single digits to 14% on highly optimized designs. For people tracking AI, the research shows the capability frontier moving from writing code to modifying hardware circuits.

The caveats: all figures are OpenAI-reported and have not been independently reproduced, and the RISC-V scoring method was defined by OpenAI. Applying this directly to your own project still requires expert review and silicon verification; it isn't production-ready the moment the model finishes.

If you work in front-end chip design or architecture, start small: pick one or two blocks, have the model rewrite the RTL, and let your existing verification flow catch issues. See whether you can reproduce the area savings or trade area for speed. If you're an investor or PM, watch what happens after AMD's manufacturing runs and how quickly the Synopsys collaboration ships. If you just want the AI progress in one line: when designing from specs, GPT-6.2 Astra scores about 0.7 on PicoRV32 and about 0.75 on Ibex—both higher than when modifying existing designs.
